principles.title: Engineering Principles
principles.subtitle: Principles I follow from experience, not trend-chasing.

p1.title: Problem Before Solution
p1.desc: I never start coding before understanding the whole problem. I ask: what am I solving? For whom? What's the cost of not solving it?

p2.title: Architecture Is Intentional
p2.desc: Every architecture decision — module separation, framework choice, organization pattern — has a reason. I don't adopt technologies because of trends.

p3.title: Simplicity by Default
p3.desc: The simplest solution that works is often the best. Complexity is only justified when the problem demands it.

p4.title: Autonomy Over Dependence
p4.desc: I build systems with fallbacks and graceful degradation when they depend on external services.

p5.title: Measure and Iterate
p5.desc: If impact cannot be measured, the scope needs another look. Every project needs metrics: time saved, processes automated, errors reduced.

p6.title: Security Is Not Optional
p6.desc: Authentication, validation, data sanitization — they're not features. They're basic requirements for any system.

p7.title: Documentation as Product
p7.desc: Every technical decision, every trade-off, every architecture choice is documented. Not for bureaucracy — for the next person who needs to understand the system.

p8.title: Tests as Guarantee
p8.desc: Tests are not overhead; they are confidence. A system without tests carries risk that is hard to see.

p9.title: Performance with Purpose
p9.desc: I optimize when the problem demands it. A dashboard that loads in 200ms is better than one that loads in 2s — but only if someone needs that speed.

p10.title: Continuous Evolution
p10.desc: No project is truly finished. Every solution has next steps, possible improvements, and trade-offs that can be re-evaluated.

p11.title: Resolution and Decision
p11.desc: Engineers solve problems. When a decision can be made with the available context, I make it and move forward responsibly.

p12.title: Ownership Over Outcome
p12.desc: The important question is whether the solution works. I take responsibility for outcomes, not only assigned tasks.

howIBuild.title: How I Build Software
howIBuild.subtitle: A real step-by-step of my engineering process.

s1.title: I Understand the Problem
s1.desc: Before any solution, I understand: who has the problem? How often? What's the cost of not solving it? What's been tried before?

s2.title: I Research Existing Solutions
s2.desc: I check if the problem has been solved before. I don't reinvent the wheel — but I also don't copy solutions that don't fit the context.

s3.title: I Design the Architecture
s3.desc: Modules, interfaces, data flow, integration points. I write before coding. A 15-minute diagram saves 15 hours of rework.

s4.title: I Define the Interfaces
s4.desc: APIs, data contracts, input/output formats. Everything typed. Everything validated. If something can be invalid, I handle it before it reaches the domain.

s5.title: I Implement in Layers
s5.desc: Domain first, infrastructure later, integration last. I don't mix responsibilities. Each layer does one thing and does it well.

s6.title: I Test Each Layer
s6.desc: Unit tests on domain, integration tests on adapters, E2E on critical flows. If I don't test it, I don't trust it.

s7.title: I Validate with Real Data
s7.desc: Nothing replaces testing with real data. Synthetic data hides problems that only appear in production.

s8.title: I Automate the Deploy
s8.desc: CI/CD, containerization, environment variables. Deploy must be automatic, reproducible, and secure.

s9.title: I Document the Decisions
s9.desc: Why did I choose X and not Y? What's the trade-off? What changes if I scale? I document decisions, not implementation.

s10.title: I Measure and Iterate
s10.desc: After launching, I measure the impact. Time saved, errors eliminated, processes automated. If I don't measure, I don't know if it worked.

behindArchitecture.title: Behind the Architecture
behindArchitecture.subtitle: The technologies I use, why I use them, and what I'd trade.

python.name: Python
python.why: Reference language for automation, data, and fast APIs. FastAPI is the framework I use most for backends.
python.tradeoff: Raw performance is lower than Go or Rust. For most cases, this doesn't matter. When it does, I optimize.

nodejs.name: Node.js
nodejs.why: npm ecosystem, HTTP APIs, React integration. I use it when I need performance in concurrent I/O.
nodejs.tradeoff: Single-threaded. For CPU-bound processing, I use Python with multiprocessing or separate workers.

nextjs.name: Next.js
nextjs.why: Server Components, SSR, automatic routes. Complete framework for web portals with SEO and performance.
nextjs.tradeoff: Complexity for simple apps. If the project is just an SPA, I use plain React with Vite.

react.name: React
react.why: Reusable components, mature ecosystem, TypeScript typing. The library I know best.
react.tradeoff: Bundle size. For static sites, I consider Astro. For simple apps, Preact.

postgresql.name: PostgreSQL
postgresql.why: Robust database, ACID, extensions, performance. For relational data, it's always my first choice.
postgresql.tradeoff: Overhead for rapid prototypes. For that, I use SQLite.

docker.name: Docker
docker.why: Reproducibility, isolation, deployment. Every system I build runs in a container.
docker.tradeoff: Setup complexity. For local prototypes, I use the runtime directly.

fastapi.name: FastAPI
fastapi.why: Fast APIs, automatic validation, generated docs. The Python framework I use most for backends.
fastapi.tradeoff: Lower maturity than Django. For apps with heavy business logic, I consider Django.
